Article Title: Asian Games 2026: PM Modi congratulates Team India, hails ‘determination, passion and remarkable sporting spirit’
Article Text:
Indian contingent at the Asian Games closing ceremony and PM Narendra Modi

‘Immense joy to the nation’

Historic golds and landmark performances

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Looking beyond Aichi-Nagoya

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday congratulated the Indian contingent for its performance at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games , praising the athletes for representing the country with “determination, passion and remarkable sporting spirit” as India concluded its campaign with 85 medals.India finished fourth on the medal table with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals, ending the Games with its second-highest medal haul in Asian Games history. The tally was 21 medals fewer than the record 106 won at the Hangzhou edition in 2023.As the Games drew to a close in Nagoya on Sunday, Modi took to X to applaud the entire contingent and the medal winners while also expressing hope that the performances would help strengthen Indian sport at the grassroots level.In his post, the Prime Minister praised the athletes for their effort and sporting spirit throughout the continental showpiece.“As the Asian Games 2026 draw to a close, my compliments to every member of the Indian contingent for representing our nation with determination, passion and remarkable sporting spirit. Congratulations to all our medal winners, whose performances have brought immense joy to the nation.May these Games inspire even greater achievements in the years ahead. May they contribute to strengthening sports at the grassroots too,” Modi wrote.The Prime Minister’s message came after more than two weeks of competition involving athletes from 45 countries. The Aichi-Nagoya Games witnessed a string of record-breaking performances, including 54 world records.The Games formally concluded with a spectacular closing ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium in Nagoya on Sunday.India’s campaign was marked by several historic performances and successful title defences across disciplines.Both Indian cricket squads retained their Asian Games titles, while the men’s and women’s kabaddi sides also won gold. The men’s hockey side successfully defended its title with a 5-1 victory over Malaysia, while the women’s team ended a 44-year wait for an Asian Games gold by defeating China 1-0 in the final.There were also several breakthrough individual performances.Pranavi Urs became the first Indian woman to win an individual Asian Games golf gold, while 17-year-old archer Kumkum Mohod created history by becoming the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold at the continental showpiece.Mohod was also part of India’s historic women’s recurve team gold that ended South Korea’s seven-edition winning streak in the event. Wrestler Sujeet Kalkal, meanwhile, produced one of the most dramatic comebacks of the Games to win the men’s 65kg freestyle gold.Boxer Lovlina Borgohain also joined an elite group of Indian women by becoming only the second after Mary Kom to win an Asian Games boxing gold.Athletics emerged as India’s biggest medal contributor with 24 medals, while shooting accounted for 15. Archery was the most successful sport in terms of gold medals, producing five top finishes.The campaign also provided a series of important milestones ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, with several young athletes making their mark on the continental stage.Earlier, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha named Mohod and Kalkal the inaugural recipients of the Jaspal Rana Award and Raja Randhir Singh Award respectively for the best female and male Indian sportspersons of the Games.With the Aichi-Nagoya campaign now complete, Modi’s message placed the emphasis not only on India’s medal tally but also on the broader legacy of the Games — inspiring another generation of athletes and strengthening the sporting ecosystem from the grassroots upwards.
Article Summary: India finished fourth on the medal table with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. The tally was 21 medals fewer than the record 106 won at the Hangzhou edition in 2023. Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised the athletes for their effort and sporting spirit throughout the continental showpiece.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: PT Usha names Kumkum Mohod, Sujeet Kalkal as Team India’s MVPs after historic golds
Article Text:
Kumkum Mohod and Sujeet Kalkal

Mohod ends South Korea’s long reign

India's Kumkum Anil Mohod (Image: REUTERS)

Kalkal turns a lost final into gold

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Sujeet Kalkal with coach after winning gold medal. (PTI Photo)

NEW DELHI: Teenage archer Kumkum Mohod and wrestler Sujeet Kalkal have been recognised as the standout performers of India’s campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, with Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha naming them the inaugural recipients of the Jaspal Rana Award and Raja Randhir Singh Award respectively.The two awards have been instituted by the IOA to honour the best female and male sportspersons of the Games and commemorate the legacy of two stalwarts of Indian sport.Seventeen-year-old Mohod, making her Asian Games debut, won three medals, including two golds, while 23-year-old Kalkal produced one of the most dramatic comebacks of the Games to claim gold in the men’s 65kg freestyle wrestling category.India finished fourth in the medal standings with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals.Mohod was at the heart of one of the biggest breakthroughs for Indian archery in Aichi-Nagoya.Along with Ankita Bhakat and Kirti, she won the women’s recurve team gold, ending South Korea’s remarkable run of seven consecutive Asian Games titles in the event dating back to the 1998 Bangkok Games.Mohod then followed it with gold in the individual recurve event, ensuring that South Korea’s women failed to win a recurve gold at the Asian Games for the first time in the discipline’s history.Her individual triumph also secured a quota place for India at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Usha praised Mohod’s ability to deliver under pressure and drew a parallel with the late Jaspal Rana, after whom the award has been named.“It is fitting that Kumkum is the first recipient of the Jaspal Rana Award, as Jaspal too burst onto the scene as a prodigy at the 1994 Asian Games. Her composure under pressure and her ability to find her best form when her back was to the wall augur extremely well for Indian Archery,” Usha said.The IOA president believes Mohod’s breakthrough could finally help Indian archery cross a long-standing barrier at the Olympics.“India's archers have been knocking on the door for more than a decade now, and I firmly believe that this performance by Kumkum and her recurve teammates has shattered the glass ceiling for Indian archery. India came close to winning a maiden Olympic medal in the sport at the Paris Olympics, and I am convinced that the final frontier will be breached at the Los Angeles Olympics,” Usha added.Kalkal, meanwhile, earned the Raja Randhir Singh Award after a gold-medal run that showcased his resilience and fighting spirit.The 23-year-old defeated reigning Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka of Japan in the semifinal before producing a stunning comeback against Abdulmazhid Kudiyev in the final.Kalkal trailed 2-9 with time running out but refused to give up, fighting back to win 10-9 in a dramatic finish. His triumph also continued India’s strong tradition in the 65kg category, following Yogeshwar Dutt and Bajrang Punia, who won Asian Games gold in the same weight class in 2014 and 2018 respectively.Usha said it was Kalkal’s refusal to accept defeat that made his performance particularly special.“Wrestling is India's sport, and Sujeet's performance will be spoken of for years to come. The gold medal will be celebrated, but his never-say-die attitude and refusal to accept silver have earned him a special place in the hearts of all Indians,” she said.“Winning gold medals in elite competition is not easy, but equally important is the effort that goes in when your back is against the wall. I wish Sujeet all success in the years ahead and will be rooting for him to deliver India's first-ever wrestling gold medal at the Olympic Games in two years' time.”The IOA will felicitate Mohod and Kalkal at a ceremony in the coming days.Their selection provides a fitting individual recognition to two athletes whose performances stood out in India’s 85-medal campaign.
Article Summary: Kumkum Mohod and Sujeet Kalkal recognised as standout performers of India’s campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. Teenage archer Mohod won three medals, including two golds, while 23-year-old KALKal produced one of the most dramatic comebacks of the Games. The two awards have been instituted by the IOA to honour the best female and male sportspersons.

Article Title: Asian Games: Leaner Indian contingent produces fewer golds but better return-per-medal - in numbers
Article Text:
Gold medallist India's players during the medal ceremony for the men's hockey event. (PTI Photo)

Where did the golds go?

Shooting, athletics behind the decline

Late surge takes India to 85 medals and fourth spot

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The overall medal gap never disappeared

In late August, the Sports Ministry maintained that the qualification criteria for the Asian Games, put into place a year ago, would not change despite criticism. “The idea, from the very beginning, was to send a lean contingent. The criteria was announced a year ago, and everyone had the time to figure it out and qualify,” a Sports Ministry source told TimesofIndia.com back then. It was made clear that the objective was to have a contingent with only realistic medal contenders making the trip to Aichi-Nagoya."Let’s take an example. If somebody has to run inside 10 seconds to be a contender for a medal in the 100m event, should we send an athlete who clocks 15 seconds? We have set the criteria that if an athlete is in the top six in Asia, we will select him or her, otherwise not. We have followed that,” the source had said.The tennis squad went from 12 to 7. Several judokas and wushu athletes were removed from the initial list. From 44 players in 2022, no footballers were sent this time. There was also no place for 20 hoopers and 16 handball players.India had sent a 661-athlete contingent to the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. Three years later, the final contingent that travelled to Japan was trimmed to 495 athletes.After 14 days of competition, India accounted for 21 golds, 27 silvers and 37 bronzes for a combined 85 medals. For comparison, India had won 106 medals in China (28 golds, 38 silvers, and 40 bronze).As the contingent size dropped by 25.1%, the golds fell by nearly the same number (25%) and medals by 19.8%. India won 16 medals for every 100 athletes in Hangzhou. In Aichi-Nagoya, that figure rose to 17.2% — an improvement of about 7.3%.Stripped to the bare bones, India won 0.172 medals per athlete in Nagoya, against 0.160 in Hangzhou. Golds per athlete were essentially unchanged at about 0.042. Crudely, it counts every athlete sent, including those who did not medal. At the same time, teams as big as cricket (30 athletes), hockey (40) and kabaddi (24) account for a single medal in a discipline.So while India did not match its record 106-medal haul, its smaller contingent produced a slightly better medal return per athlete.The more complicated part of the comparison comes when gold medals are brought into the mix.India's gold medal tally fell from 28 to 21, a 25% decline — exactly in line with the reduction in the size of the contingent. The gold-medal yield was therefore virtually unchanged: 4.24 golds per 100 athletes in Hangzhou and 4.24 in Aichi-Nagoya.That suggests the smaller contingent was not, by itself, the reason India's gold tally fell. Rather, the composition of the medal haul changed.India's 2022 golds came heavily from three sports: shooting (seven), athletics (six), and archery (five), which is 18 of 28 (64%). In Nagoya, archery again delivered five, but shooting produced three and athletics one. Boxing, which won no gold in Hangzhou, won three, and wrestling won two after none. Golf added a gold courtesy Pranavi Urs. Squash, which won two golds in 2022, won none, despite the expectations from Anahat Singh, though the overall count of five medals did not change.The team sports carried more of the load. Cricket, hockey and kabaddi won six of India's 21 golds, up from five of 28. India completed a double title finish in all three. In 2022, hockey had produced one gold and one bronze.Athletics' podium shifted down a step. In 2022, it returned six golds, 14 silvers and nine bronzes. Now, despite a massive 75-plus-member contingent, it produced one gold, nine silvers and 14 bronzes.Shooting (4) and athletics (5) were the biggest reasons behind the drop in gold medals. Squash (2), Badminton (1), Tennis (1) and Equestrian (1) all also witnessed a drop in the yellow metal. Tennis, in fact, didn't produce a medal at all - a first in 40 years.In Hangzhou, shooting and athletics were the two biggest contributors to India's gold medal tally, producing seven and six gold medals, respectively. Together, they accounted for 13 of India's 28 golds. In Aichi-Nagoya, that combined figure collapsed to four. Shooting contributed three golds, while athletics produced one. India therefore lost nine gold medals from these two sports alone.The sub-par show from the athletes was made murkier by the withdrawals of 100m hurdler Jyothi Yarraji and triple jumper Praveen Chithravel. Both national record holders had skipped the Indian Athletics Series Final in prelude to the Asian Games, citing knee stress and a calf muscle pull, respectively.When it came to the Asian Games, Yarraji pulled out of the women's 100m hurdles first-round heats after "feeling pain" during the warm-up under rainy conditions.Chithravel, meanwhile, attempted his first jump but could not complete it, exiting the competition area clutching his calf in apparent pain. He was later taken away in a wheelchair. Men's 400m hurdler Yashas P., too, pulled out after starting his Heat.Coming to the shooters.India's 2026 shooting tally of 15 medals (3 golds, 8 silvers and 4 bronzes) was a 32% drop in total medal tally when compared to 22 in the previous continental showpiece. The gold haul took a 57% hit. Broken further, seven were team medals, five individual and three in mixed team events.The gold medals came in one individual (Neeru Dhanda in women's trap) and two mixed team events (Neeru and Kynan Chenai in mixed trap and Suruchi Phogat and Kamaljeet in mixed 10m air pistol).If the final medal tally tells one story, the daily trajectory tells another. Through the first 12 days of competition, India had won 10 gold medals in Aichi-Nagoya. In Hangzhou, India had already accumulated 21 golds by the same point.Then came the late surge in Japan.India won 11 gold medals over the final two days of its 2026 campaign — six on Day 13 and five on Day 14. That means 52.4% of India's entire gold haul came in the final two days. The equivalent figure in Hangzhou was 25%: seven of India's 28 golds came during the final two days.India had 13 golds by Day 8 in Hangzhou. At the same stage in Aichi-Nagoya, it had four. By Day 11, the gap was still eight golds — 18 to 10.But the final stretch changed the picture dramatically. India collected 18 golds across Days 13 and 14 in the two editions combined, but the distribution was very different: seven in Hangzhou and 11 in Aichi-Nagoya.On October 2, the women's recurve team of Ankita Bhakat, Kirti Sharma and Kumkum Mohod picked a gold. As did boxer Lovlina Borgohain on her birthday. Parveen Hooda also joined the party alongside wrestler Sujeet Kalkal's remarkable comeback, boxer Ankush Panghal's drought-ending gold, and the women's hockey team's triumph over China to seal an LA 2028 spot.A day later, archer Kumkum Mohod, golfer Pranavi Urs, wrestler Aman Sehrawat, the men's cricket team, and the men's hockey team gave the country plenty to celebrate with golden flourishes.The same late surge was visible in the total medal count, but it was not enough to close the gap with Hangzhou.After the first day, India had five medals in Hangzhou and two in Aichi-Nagoya.By Day 4, the difference had grown to 10 medals.By Day 8, it was 16.By Day 11, Hangzhou's cumulative tally stood at 80 medals, compared with 60 in Aichi-Nagoya — a 20-medal gap.India narrowed that deficit slightly over the next two days, reaching 76 medals against Hangzhou's 94 after Day 13.But the final day added nine medals in Aichi-Nagoya and 12 in Hangzhou, leaving the final difference to 21.
Article Summary: India had sent a 661-athlete contingent to the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. Three years later, the final contingent that travelled to Japan was trimmed to 495 athletes. India accounted for 21 golds, 27 silvers and 37 bronzes for a combined 85 medals. For comparison, India had won 106 medals in China.

Article Title: ‘Learn from these Games and keep moving forward’: Abhinav Bindra’s message to Team India as LA Olympics beckons
Article Text:
Indian athletes leave the arena following the closing ceremony for the Asian Games in Nagoya. (AP Photo)

'Enormous respect to our athletes'

'LA is less than two years away'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Olympic gold medallist Abhinav Bindra has urged Indian athletes to learn from both the successes and disappointments of the Asian Games 2026, calling for stronger high-performance systems and a renewed focus on preparations for the Los Angeles Olympics, which are less than two years away.Congratulating India's athletes and support teams after the country finished fourth in the Aichi-Nagoya Games with 85 medals, Bindra highlighted the years of hard work and sacrifices behind their performances while stressing the need for an honest assessment of the campaign.India finished with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals, falling short of its record haul of 106 medals at Hangzhou 2023. However, the campaign produced several historic achievements, including gold-medal sweeps in men's and women's cricket, kabaddi and hockey.In a lengthy post on X on Sunday, Bindra thanked athletes, their families, coaches and support staff for their contributions before urging the sporting establishment to turn the lessons from Aichi-Nagoya into meaningful improvements."Congratulations to every Indian athlete and to Team India on the Asian Games. A Games campaign is never just the few days we see on television. It is years of early mornings, injuries, doubts, missed occasions and countless hours of work," Bindra wrote."So first and foremost, enormous respect to our athletes and also to their families who live this journey with them and make sacrifices that are rarely seen. To the coaches, support staff, federations, SAI, the Government and everyone working behind the scenes, THANK YOU!"The 2008 Beijing Olympics gold medallist in shooting acknowledged the breakthrough performances in Aichi-Nagoya, particularly those of young athletes who announced themselves on the continental stage. However, he stressed that disappointments must also be examined rather than simply forgotten."There have been some terrific breakthrough performances at these Games. Young athletes have announced themselves, others have stepped up to a new level, and there have been moments that give us a lot to be excited about. There have also been disappointments. That is sport, and every Games will have them. What matters now is how honestly we learn from them," he added.Bindra called for a more comprehensive approach to athlete development, arguing that high-performance programmes must provide the right expertise throughout an athlete's career rather than stepping in only when medals are within reach."High performance cannot only be about reacting when an athlete is close to a medal. We have to keep building systems that understand the athlete over several years," he wrote.He emphasised the importance of sports science, data-driven decisions, coaching, competition planning, training-load management, recovery and injury prevention, alongside building physical and mental resilience."Most importantly, the right expertise has to reach the athlete at the right stage of their career, not when it is already too late," he said.With the next Summer Olympics approaching, Bindra warned that the preparation window was shrinking and called for immediate action."LA is less than two years away. In Olympic sport, that is not a long time. The athletes who will stand on the podium there are already deep into their preparation today."His message was to celebrate the achievements, acknowledge shortcomings and return to work with renewed determination."Be proud of what has been achieved. Learn from these Games and keep moving forward. Wishing Team India everything good on the road to LA," he concluded.
Article Summary: Bindra urges Indian athletes to learn from successes and disappointments of the Asian Games 2026. Olympic gold medallist calls for stronger high-performance systems and a renewed focus on preparations for the Los Angeles Olympics. India finished with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals, falling short of its record haul of 106 medals at Hangzhou 2023.

Article Title: Asian Games: Olympic Council of Asia cites 54 world records to declare Aichi-Nagoya Games a success despite chaos
Article Text:
Ri Song Gum of North Korea had a sweep of world records at 49kg on 94-121-215. (AP Photo)

President of the OCA, Sheikh Joaan Bin Hamad Al Thani, left, looks at the Olympic Council of Asia flag as Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, PM of Qatar holds it. (AP Photo)

OCA highlights records, revenue growth

Logistical problems remain a concern

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) has defended the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games as a success, pointing to 54 world records, strong viewership and a nearly 20% increase in revenue despite persistent logistical problems that marred the continental sporting showpiece.OCA Director General Husain Al-Musallam said the record-breaking performances demonstrated that athletes had the environment needed to deliver exceptional results during the Games, which concluded on Sunday.A total of 54 world records, 11 junior world records and 89 continental records were set during the competition, providing the OCA with evidence of the event's sporting success despite complaints over accommodation and transportation."This achievement does not come without the best environment," Al-Musallam told reporters at a press conference on the final day of the Games."The athletes cannot perform if they don't have transportation. The athletes cannot perform if they don't have good healthcare. The athletes cannot perform if they don't eat food. Number talks, it's evidence. We are here to present you with the evidence."Al-Musallam also highlighted the financial sustainability of the Aichi-Nagoya model, arguing that major sporting events did not necessarily require expensive infrastructure projects that could become underused after the competition."We are happy to see that there is no big financial burden in the organising committee, and there is no white elephant staying in Nagoya or any place," he said.The OCA attributed the nearly 20% revenue increase compared with the Hangzhou 2023 Asian Games largely to digital growth and stronger viewership. India's hockey and cricket matches against Pakistan were among the fixtures that attracted large television audiences.Weightlifting was a major contributor to the record-breaking spectacle, with 25 senior world records established in the sport. North Korea led the way with 15 world records, while China also produced a series of outstanding performances.The Games attracted around 17,000 athletes and officials following a surge in late entries, approximately 2,000 more than initially projected.The sporting achievements, however, came against a backdrop of organisational difficulties. Without a dedicated athletes' village, participants were accommodated in hotels, container-style living units and a cruise ship.The unexpected increase in registrations strained accommodation and transport arrangements, prompting complaints about cramped rooms, small beds and unreliable transportation. Organising committee secretary general Satoshi Murate apologised for the problems.OCA officials nevertheless argued that the Games demonstrated the power of sport to bring countries together amid international tensions."When you look to the news, conflict everywhere - in Asia, outside Asia," Al-Musallam said. "Economic problems everywhere. But look at Asia, how united we are in sport."Tayyab Ikram, chairman of the Games Coordination Committee, acknowledged that improvements were necessary."There is no Games without challenges. There are no Games without initial interruptions," Ikram said."In the future, we would like to see more sustainable solutions, more improvement and innovation ... but without compromising on the athletes' conditions."As Doha prepares to host the 2030 Asian Games, the Aichi-Nagoya edition has left organisers with two contrasting legacies: a remarkable collection of sporting records and a reminder that operational efficiency must match athletic ambition.
Article Summary: OCA defends Aichi-Nagoya 2026 as a success despite logistical problems. 54 world records, 11 junior world records and 89 continental records set during competition. North Korea led the way with 15 world records while China also produced a series of outstanding performances.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026 MVPs: Meet teenage sensation Yu Zidi and sprint king Puripol Boonson
Article Text:
Yu Zidi and Puripol Boonson (Reuters/AP Photo)

Yu Zidi: Teen sensation makes history

Yu Zidi of China (AP Photo)

Boonson: Thailand's sprint king

Stars with Los Angeles in sight

The Asian Games have found two new superstars.China's 13-year-old swimming sensation Yu Zidi and Thailand's 20-year-old sprinting powerhouse Puripol Boonson were named the Female and Male Most Valuable Players of the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games by the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) on Sunday.The pair were rewarded for spectacular campaigns in which they combined multiple gold medals with a string of Asian Games and Asian records, emerging as two of the brightest young stars of the continental showpiece.Yu and Boonson will each receive USD 25,000 from the OCA for their performances.Yu was one of the breakout stars of Aichi-Nagoya, winning three individual gold medals at just 13 years of age and becoming the youngest MVP in Asian Games history.Her golden run began in the women's 200m butterfly, where she clocked 2:05.08 on September 20 to set a new Games Record.A day later, she produced an even more impressive performance in the women's 200m individual medley. Her time of 2:06.10 set a new Games Record and lowered the Asian Record.Yu completed her hat-trick on September 23, winning the women's 400m individual medley in 4:28.56, another Games Record.Three events, three golds and four records made the Chinese teenager one of the defining faces of the Games.If Yu ruled the pool, Boonson owned the track.The 20-year-old Thai sprinter stormed to a 100m-200m double, setting four Asian Games Records and equalling an Asian Record during his campaign.In the men's 100m, Boonson first broke the Games Record with 9.91 seconds in the semifinal before going even faster in the final, clocking 9.90 seconds to claim gold on September 25.Two days later, he completed the sprint double in the 200m. His winning time of 19.88 seconds broke his own Games Record of 20.10 seconds and equalled the Asian Record.He also added a silver medal in Thailand's mixed 4x100m relay, further underlining his impact in Aichi-Nagoya.The OCA MVP Awards Panel said the selection was particularly difficult because of the exceptional quality of performances across the Games.Tayyab Ikram, chair of the five-member panel, said Yu and Boonson had established themselves as "Asian sports superstars" and backed them to achieve even greater success at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.Their selection places them alongside a distinguished list of previous Asian Games MVPs, including Japan's Koji Ito and Kosuke Kitajima, China's Lin Dan and Rikako Ikee, and the 2022 winners Qin Haiyang and Zhang Yufei.For Yu, still only 13, and Boonson, at 20, Aichi-Nagoya could prove to be only the beginning. The Asian Games gave the continent two spectacular new stars — and a glimpse of what could lie ahead on the Olympic stage.

The pair were rewarded for spectacular campaigns in which they combined multiple gold medals with a string of Asian Games and Asian records. They will each receive USD 25,000 from the OCA for their performances.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: Curtain comes down in Aichi-Nagoya as Doha receives flag for 2030 edition
Article Text:
India contingent during the athletes parade at the closing ceremony. (Reuters Photo)

India finishes fourth with 85 medals

India's flag bearer Neeru Dhanda and others during the closing ceremony. (PTI Photo)

Doha receives the baton for 2030

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Qatar equestrian athlete Jassim Al Kuwari rides with the Olympic Council of Asia flag during the closing ceremony. (AP Photo)

Sporting brilliance amid organisational challenges

The 20th Asian Games came to a glittering close on Sunday, bringing down the curtain on more than two weeks of sporting action in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, as Qatar received the flag for the next edition in Doha in 2030. Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) President Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani officially declared the Games closed at Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium, marking the end of a sporting spectacle that celebrated Asia's athletic excellence.Thousands of athletes, officials and spectators gathered for the closing ceremony, which carried the theme 'One Asia'. The proceedings also featured the formal handover to Qatari representatives, with Doha preparing to host the continent's premier multi-sport event four years from now.India's Neeru Dhanda, who enjoyed a memorable campaign with two gold medals and a silver in shooting, carried the national flag at the ceremony, capping a landmark outing for the Indian contingent.India signed off with 85 medals — 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze — to finish fourth in the overall standings, behind China, Japan and South Korea.The campaign featured significant performances across shooting, athletics, boxing, hockey and other disciplines, underlining India's growing depth across sports.Neeru's outstanding haul was among the highlights, while India's gold-medal-winning hockey campaigns secured qualifications for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.India's performance also continued a broader trend of consistent medal hauls at recent Asian Games, following the historic 100-medal milestone at Hangzhou 2023. The Aichi-Nagoya edition offered further evidence of the country's expanding presence across the continental sporting landscape, even as the final tally fell short of the previous edition's overall medal count.The closing ceremony formally shifted attention to the next host city, with Doha set to welcome Asia's sporting community in 2030. The handover marked the beginning of preparations for Qatar's second Asian Games, following its hosting of the event in 2006.The Aichi-Nagoya Games featured 469 gold-medal events across a record programme of 43 sports, with around 17,000 athletes and officials participating. Several disciplines, including padel, mixed martial arts, teqball and surfing, made their Asian Games debuts, reflecting the event's evolving sporting landscape.China dominated the standings with 169 gold medals among 341 medals overall, recording its best gold-medal haul at an Asian Games held outside its home territory. Hosts Japan finished second with 83 golds and 269 medals, surpassing their previous gold-medal record at Hiroshima 1994.Despite the on-field excitement, the Games faced criticism over accommodation and transport arrangements. Organisers opted against building a dedicated athletes' village, instead using hotels, modular accommodation and a cruise ship to house participants.Registration delays, room-allocation problems and unreliable shuttle services affected several delegations, while diplomatic and ceremonial mix-ups added to the difficulties. Attendance was also subdued at several venues, with accessibility issues contributing to disappointing crowds.Nevertheless, the competition produced several remarkable individual performances, led by China's teenage swimming sensation Yu Zidi and seven-gold winner Zhang Zhanshuo, alongside standout displays in athletics and other disciplines.As Aichi-Nagoya handed over the baton to Doha, the Games closed with a celebration of sporting achievement, even as the organisational shortcomings offered important lessons for the next edition.
Article Summary: The 20th Asian Games came to a glittering close in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. Qatar received the flag for the next edition in Doha in 2030. China dominated the standings with 169 gold medals among 341 medals overall. Hosts Japan finished second with 83 golds and 269 medals.

Article Title: ‘Pakistan don’t offer much competition’: BCCI takes swipe after Asian Games final
Article Text:
India's team holds the national flag as they celebrate after winning the final T20I cricket match against Pakistan(PTI Photo)

Abhishek sets the tone, Tilak finishes strongly

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bowlers hold their nerve

BCCI president Mithun Manhas praised India’s handling of pressure in the Asian Games 2026 men’s cricket final against Pakistan , while taking a dig at the quality of competition offered by the arch-rivals in recent years.India secured one of their 21 gold medals at the Games after beating Pakistan by 19 runs in the final on Saturday, October 3, at the Korakuen Stadium in Nisshin, Japan. The closely fought contest saw Pakistan push India hard during the chase, but the defending champions held their nerve to retain the gold medal.Manhas, however, felt the result also highlighted what he believes is a decline in the competitiveness of India-Pakistan contests.“They defeated arch-rivals Pakistan, who I feel don't offer much competition anymore, and the way our team handled pressure situations... no other team in the world can do that," Manhas said after the final.The BCCI president also lauded India’s overall campaign, insisting that the team deserved its status as the tournament’s best side."By far the best team of the tournament. We are the defending champions, and the performance they have shown this time is commendable,” he added.Abhishek Sharma and Tilak Varma played key roles in India’s imposing total of 211, with both batters registering half-centuries.Manhas highlighted the contribution of the two batters and explained how India’s top and middle order combined to put Pakistan under pressure.“This is a team sport. Tilak Varma batted brilliantly, and Abhishek Sharma set the tone for the game. The job of openers is to build the innings, and the middle order finishes it. So, the openers basically set the tone," Manhas said.Abhishek gave India an explosive start, scoring 61 off 28 balls, while Tilak struck 51 off 22. India lost wickets during the middle overs but recovered through Tilak and Shivam Dube, who added 62 runs off 30 balls for the sixth wicket.“Team India's batting has been tremendous, and as for the bowling, I would say everyone contributed together to defend a good total,” the former Delhi batter added.India’s 211 was the first total above 200 in the tournament. Pakistan, though, mounted a serious challenge in the chase, led by Hasan Nawaz, who smashed 96 off 51 deliveries.India’s bowlers eventually managed to keep Pakistan to 182/6 after 20 overs, securing a 19-run victory. Axar Patel and Washington Sundar claimed two wickets each, while Jasprit Bumrah went wicketless but played a crucial role by bowling effectively during tense phases of the chase.The victory gave India back-to-back Asian Games cricket gold medals after their triumph in the previous edition.
Article Summary: India secured one of their 21 gold medals at the Games after beating Pakistan by 19 runs in the final on Saturday, October 3, at the Korakuen Stadium in Nisshin, Japan. The victory gave India back-to-back Asian Games cricket gold medals after their triumph in the previous edition.

Article Title: 20 Hangzhou golds gone, 13 new routes to gold: How India’s Asian Games medal map changed

Firsts for India at Asian Games 2026

The gold rush was not simply a repeat

India Found 13 New Golds

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India won 28 gold medals at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. Four years later, the question in Aichi-Nagoya was how many of those titles it could retain. The answer? - Eight, out of the 28 Hangzhou golds. That’s 28.6 per cent of the total. Twenty titles changed hands.The biggest changes came in the sports that had driven India's record campaign in Hangzhou. All seven shooting golds were lost, while all six athletics titles changed hands and, India also failed to retain either of its two individual compound archery golds.But just the gold-medal count does not tell the whole story. India retained the three compound team archery titles, both kabaddi golds, both cricket titles and the men's hockey crown.The other golds came from a different mix of events and athletes. Some had won silver or bronze in Hangzhou and moved up to gold in Japan. Others won titles in events where India had not been on the podium four years earlier.So while 20 of India's 28 Hangzhou champions failed to retain their titles, the gold medals themselves were replaced from a much wider pool. The Aichi-Nagoya campaign, in that sense, was less about defending the Hangzhou haul and more about how India's medal map had changed in four years.While Shooting had produced seven golds and 22 medals for India at Hangzhou, In Aichi-Nagoya, the overall medal tally fell to 15. The gold count dropped from seven to three, while silver moved from nine to eight and bronze from six to four. The biggest change was that none of India's seven Hangzhou golds was defended in the same event.Instead, India found gold elsewhere. Neeru Dhanda won the women's trap individual title and then partnered Kynan Chenai to win mixed trap. Kamaljeet and Suruchi Singh added the mixed 10m air pistol gold.The rifle teams that had delivered two of India's Hangzhou golds - men's 10m air rifle and men's 50m rifle 3 Positions - returned with silver in Japan. There was also a new medal in mixed skeet. Anantjeet Singh Naruka and Parinaaz Dhaliwal won bronze, giving India its first Asian Games medal in the event.So while India's shooting haul was smaller in Aichi-Nagoya, the change was not just in the numbers. The seven golds from Hangzhou were gone, and the three titles in Japan came from a different set of events.While India won 29 athletics medals in Hangzhou, Four years later, the tally in Aichi-Nagoya was 24. The bigger change, though, came in the gold count.Six golds in Hangzhou became one in Japan and that lone title came in the women's 4x400m relay, four years after India's men's relay team had won gold in Hangzhou. Silver medals fell from 14 to nine, while bronze medals increased from nine to 14.There was still plenty of continuity among India's medallists. Murali Sreeshankar again won silver in the long jump. Tajinderpal Singh Toor, the Hangzhou gold medallist, finished with silver this time. Tejaswin Shankar moved from silver to bronze in the decathlon, while Ancy Sojan retained her long-jump silver.Vithya Ramraj again won bronze in the 400m hurdles. Gulveer Singh improved on his Hangzhou performance in the 10,000m, moving from bronze to silver. He also added silver in the 1500m and bronze in the 5000m.So the athletics podium did not disappear in Aichi-Nagoya. India still won 23 medals outside gold. The difference was that performances that had produced six titles in Hangzhou produced only one gold four years later.India matched its Hangzhou tally in archery, winning nine medals again - five gold, two silver and two bronze. The medal distribution, however, changed considerably.The three compound team golds were retained and beyond those events, India had a different set of medal-winning performances in Aichi-Nagoya, particularly in the women's recurve events.Kumkum Mohod won individual recurve gold, while the women's recurve team moved from bronze in Hangzhou to gold in Japan. That left the overall numbers unchanged, but the events behind those numbers were different.The individual compound events also saw a change. India had won medals in both the men's and women's individual compound events in Hangzhou. In Aichi-Nagoya, the men's individual compound event was the notable gap.Boxing went in the opposite direction to shooting and athletics. India had returned from Hangzhou with four medals - one silver and three bronze - but no gold, but In Aichi-Nagoya, the haul rose to six, including three gold medals.Lovlina Borgohain upgraded her silver in the women's 75kg category in 2023, to gold four years later, while Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal added two more titles in categories where India had not won gold at Hangzhou. The bronze tally remained unchanged at three.Wrestling also finished with six medals, the same tally as Hangzhou. But the distribution changed completely. India had won one silver and five bronze medals in 2022, without a gold. In Aichi-Nagoya, that became two golds, two silvers and two bronze medals.Aman Sehrawat and Sujeet Kalkal supplied the two freestyle golds, while Nitesh, added a historic silver in Greco-Roman, and Antim Panghal upgraded her bronze from the 2022 Games to silver in 2026.The bronze tally fell from five to two (Sunil Kumar and Deepak Punia), but India added two golds and one silver.Squash finished with five medals in both Hangzhou and Aichi-Nagoya. But the two golds from 2022 were gone.India's tally changed from two gold, one silver and two bronze to two silver and three bronze. Abhay Singh retained the men's singles silver, replacing Saurav Ghosal on the podium. Anahat Singh added a women's singles medal.The men's team and mixed doubles titles from Hangzhou slipped to bronze in Japan. The women's team retained its bronze, while the mixed-team bronze was not repeated. The overall medal count stayed at five. The two golds did not.India had won all four golds available across the two sports in Hangzhou - the men's and women's cricket titles and the men's and women's kabaddi titles and it repeated that sweep in Japan.In the kabaddi double, both Indian teams came through against Iran in the finals, with the women winning 37-34 and the men 40-34. For the women's team, the victory extended an impressive Asian Games record. India has now won the women's kabaddi gold at every edition it has entered except the 2018 Jakarta Games, when Iran took the title and India settled for silver. The 2026 victory was therefore its fourth gold in five appearances.The men's side has an even longer record. India's 40-34 win over Iran was its ninth Asian Games gold in the men's event across 10 editions. The only time it failed to win the title was in 2018, when Iran took gold. India had returned to the top at Hangzhou and retained the crown in Nagoya.Cricket followed with its own repeat. India's women's team opened the 2026 Games by defending the title it had won at Hangzhou, beating Sri Lanka in the final. The men's team then completed the cricket double on October 3, beating Pakistan to retain the men's gold as well.Hockey produced two very different stories in Aichi-Nagoya. The men's gold was defended. The women's bronze became gold.For the men's team, the 2026 title was significant beyond the medal itself. India beat Malaysia 5-1 in the final to retain the Asian Games crown for the first time, becoming only the second country after Pakistan to win consecutive men's hockey golds. The victory also secured direct qualification for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.The women's title was a different story altogether. India had finished with bronze in Hangzhou. In Japan, it beat defending champions China 1-0 to win the Asian Games gold for the first time since 1982. The victory ended a 44-year wait for gold and also secured direct qualification for LA 2028.It also produced a first for Indian hockey at the Asian Games. For the first time, both the men's and women's teams won gold at the same edition.At Hangzhou, Aditi Ashok won silver, giving India its first women's golf medal at the Asian Games. Four years later, Pranavi Urs went one better.She won individual gold, becoming the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games golf title. Urs then joined Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar to win India's first women's team medal in the sport. India's overall golf haul doubled from one medal in Hangzhou to two in Aichi-Nagoya.The individual gold also ended a 24-year wait for India. Shiv Kapur had won the men's title in 2002; Pranavi became the first Indian golfer since then to win an individual Asian Games gold.Sailing: Three medals again, but different eventsSailing produced the same number of medals in both editions. India won three medals in Hangzhou and three again in Aichi-Nagoya. But the events behind those medals changed.Two new skiff events produced podium finishes in Japan, replacing the men's windsurfer and men's dinghy medals from Hangzhou. The women's dinghy medal also changed colour, from silver to bronze.Badminton saw one of India's biggest drops between Hangzhou and Aichi-Nagoya. The medal tally fell from three to one. India's 2022 haul included Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty's men's doubles gold, the men's team silver and HS Prannoy's singles bronze.Four years later, the men's team remained India's only podium finisher. But even that medal changed colour, with the silver becoming bronze.Neither of the two individual medals from Hangzhou was defended. There was no individual podium finish in Aichi-Nagoya, leaving India with just one medal from a sport that had produced three in the previous edition.Rowing's fall was even more pronounced. Five medals in Hangzhou became one bronze in Aichi-Nagoya. In 2022, India had taken two silver and three bronze medals across five events. In Japan, only Satnam Singh and Salman Khan's men's double sculls reached the podium.None of the five events that had delivered medals at Hangzhou did so again. And the build-up itself was unsettled, with last-minute changes to crew combinations and event entries. Arvind Singh, a 2022 silver medallist in the lightweight double sculls, was moved into the quadruple sculls, while Balraj Panwar shifted from the quadruple to the single sculls.Tennis went from two medals in Hangzhou to none in Aichi-Nagoya. The bigger change was the end of India's 36-year medal streak at the Asian Games.India had continued to find tennis medals across different generations, from Leander Paes and Mahesh Bhupathi to Sania Mirza, Rohan Bopanna and the current doubles players. That run ended in Japan.India had three quarterfinal opportunities but could not convert any of them into a medal. Sumit Nagal went out in the singles quarterfinals, while India did not have a women's singles entry. The result was India's first medal-less Asian Games tennis campaign since 1986.Equestrian went from two medals in Hangzhou to none in Aichi-Nagoya. India had won one gold and one bronze in 2022. There was no podium finish this time.The campaign was also affected by selection disputes, the absence of an approved show-jumping team and a setback in eventing. The result was a complete reversal from Hangzhou, with a two-medal haul turning into none in Japan.Aichi-Nagoya also added two new sports to India's Asian Games medal list. Suchika Tariyal won bronze in the women's traditional MMA 60kg category, giving India its first Asian Games medal in mixed martial arts.Jay Meena added another first in soft tennis, winning bronze in men's singles. For Meena, the medal came after two previous Asian Games appearances without a podium finish. He had competed at the 2018 and 2022 Games but returned without a medal on both occasions. In Nagoya, he finally reached the podium.Neither medal replaced a gold lost from Hangzhou. They came from sports that had not previously contributed an Asian Games medal to India.Weightlifting produced another long-gap story. Mirabai Chanu's silver in the women's 49kg category was India's first Asian Games weightlifting medal since Karnam Malleswari's silver at Bangkok 1998.There was also a personal milestone. Chanu had Olympic and World Championship medals and Commonwealth Games titles, but an Asian Games medal had remained missing. The silver in Nagoya completed the collection.India had not won a kurash medal at the previous Asian Games. Pincky Balhara put the sport back on India's medal list in Aichi-Nagoya, winning bronze in the women's -78kg category. It was a return to the podium rather than a title defence, adding another sport to India's 2026 medal tally.Wushu, Table Tennis, sepak takraw: Medals from the wider fieldWushu again produced a medal through Roshibina Devi, who won silver in the women's 60kg sanda - her third Asian Games medal.Table tennis added bronze through Diya Chitale and Manush Shah in mixed doubles, while World No.3 men’s pair of Manush Shah and Manav Thakar flattered to deceive.India also retained its bronze in sepak takraw, with the men's quadrant team finishing on the podium again.The other side: Four sports drop out of India's medal listThe Hangzhou-to-Aichi-Nagoya comparison also has a different side. Some sports that had contributed medals in 2022 did not produce one in Japan.Chess, bridge, roller sports and canoeing had together contributed six medals to India's Hangzhou tally - two silver in chess, one silver in bridge, two bronze in roller sports and one bronze in canoeing. None of those four sports were part of the Aichi-Nagoya programme.The changing medal map also showed up in the number of firsts India recorded in Aichi-Nagoya.Thirteen of India's 2026 gold medals came from events in which India had either won silver or bronze at Hangzhou, or had not won a medal at all. That included three shooting golds.The mixed 10m air pistol moved from silver to gold, while Neeru Dhanda won the women's individual trap and mixed trap titles in events where India had not won gold in Hangzhou.Athletics produced another upgrade, with the women's 4x400m relay moving from silver to gold.Archery's women's recurve team went from bronze to gold, while Kumkum Mohod added the individual recurve title.Boxing produced three more. Lovlina Borgohain moved from silver to gold in the women's 75kg category. Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal won titles in categories where India had not taken gold in Hangzhou.Wrestling followed the same pattern. Sujeet Kalkal won the men's 65kg title, while Aman Sehrawat moved from bronze in 2022 to gold in the 57kg category.In golf, Pranavi Urs turned Aditi Ashok's women's individual silver from Hangzhou into gold. Women's hockey completed another major upgrade, moving from bronze in Hangzhou to gold in Aichi-Nagoya.Taken together, these 13 golds explain why the 2026 campaign cannot be judged simply by counting how many Hangzhou champions retained their titles.India did lose 20 of its 28 Hangzhou golds, but several of those losses were replaced by athletes who had finished lower on the podium in 2022, or had not reached it at all.The fact that India defended only eight of its 28 Hangzhou golds does not mean the 2026 campaign simply replaced the previous one with a broader or better model. Hangzhou had a heavy concentration of gold at the top. Shooting won seven. Athletics won six. Archery won five. Together, those three disciplines accounted for 18 of India's 28 gold medals in 2022. That made Hangzhou's medal profile very different from Aichi-Nagoya.And the disciplines that lost the most golds in Japan did not disappear from the podium. Shooting remained one of India's biggest medal contributors with 15 medals. Athletics produced 24, while archery matched its Hangzhou total of nine. So the change was not that India's traditional strengths stopped producing medals. They simply produced fewer golds.
Article Summary: India won 28 gold medals at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. Twenty per cent of the total gold medals changed hands. India's record was broken with seven golds in shooting. All six athletics titles changed hands, while all six cricket titles also failed to retain.

5. Table tennis, fencing, esports, rowing all disappoint

India signed off from the Asian Games 2026 in fourth place with 85 medals — 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze. The final tally was below the record 106 medals won at Hangzhou, but a strong finish in the final days changed the complexion of the campaign.From Kumkum Mohod’s historic archery gold and Aman Sehrawat’s wrestling triumph to disappointing campaigns in tennis and some traditionally strong disciplines, India’s Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games journey had its share of soaring highs and hard misses.Here are India's biggest hits and flops from Aichi-Nagoya.Archery was arguably India's biggest success story when it came to gold medals.India won five gold medals, with the women's and men's compound teams, mixed compound team, women's recurve team and Kumkum Mohod's individual recurve triumph providing the highlights.The biggest moment came from 17-year-old Kumkum Mohod, who became the first Indian woman to win an individual recurve gold at the Asian Games.Her success, along with the women's recurve team's gold, gave Indian archery a memorable Games. Kumkum also added a silver in the mixed recurve team event with Dhiraj Bommadevara.Indian hockey delivered when it mattered most.The women's team ended a 44-year wait for an Asian Games gold, while Harmanpreet Singh's men's team defeated Malaysia 5-1 in the final to retain the title.The two victories also had an Olympic dimension, with India's performances securing qualification opportunities for Los Angeles 2028.The men's final was the perfect way to close India's medal campaign, with the 5-1 victory delivering the country's 21st gold.India's cricket teams delivered two more gold medals.The women's team retained its title, while the men's side defeated Pakistan by 19 runs in the final to successfully defend India's Asian Games crown. Abhishek Sharma's explosive batting and Tilak Varma's unbeaten 51 were among the highlights of the men's final.The men's final also became one of the most talked-about sporting moments of the Games, thanks to the India-Pakistan rivalry.India's boxers produced one of the strongest late surges of the Games, winning three gold medals.Lovlina Borgohain, Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal emerged as champions in their respective categories.For Lovlina, the victory was particularly significant: she became only the second Indian woman after Mary Kom to win an Asian Games boxing gold.Aman Sehrawat's gold was one of the more compelling individual stories of the Games.The wrestler had endured a difficult period involving illness, absences and a loss of motivation following the Paris Olympics. His return to the top at Aichi-Nagoya turned the campaign into a personal comeback story as well as a medal-winning one.India finished with two wrestling golds, along with silver and bronze medals.Pranavi Urs created history by winning India's first women's individual golf gold at the Asian Games.India also took silver in the women's team event, making golf one of the country's notable success stories in Aichi-Nagoya.Kabaddi remained one of India's most dependable gold-medal sports at Aichi-Nagoya.Both the men's and women's teams won gold, allowing India to retain its titles and reinforce its dominance in the sport at the Asian Games.The double triumph was another strong performance from a discipline where India continues to set the continental benchmark.Athletics was India's biggest contributor by overall medal count, producing 24 medals.The medal haul included silver medals for Ancy Sojan, Sarvesh Kushare, Sawan Berwal, Gulveer Singh and others, along with multiple bronze medals across track and field.The sport also produced historic moments, including Baranica Elangovan's first-ever Asian Games pole-vault medal for India and Vithya Ramraj's national-record bronze in the 400m hurdles.The caveat is the gold count. Athletics produced a huge volume of medals but only one gold, meaning the sport's conversion into top-of-the-podium finishes remains an area India will want to improve.Tennis was arguably India's biggest disappointment.For the first time in four decades, India failed to win a single Asian Games tennis medal. The campaign ended without a podium finish despite the country's historically strong record in the sport at the continental event.The result was particularly striking because tennis has traditionally been one of India's reliable Asian Games medal sports.Shooting eventually contributed 15 medals, including three golds, making it one of India's biggest medal-producing sports.But the campaign began with considerable disappointment.India endured several fourth-place finishes and missed opportunities before Suruchi Singh and Kamaljeet finally ended the wait for a shooting gold.Tilottama Sen and Vidarsa Vinod, for example, finished fourth and fifth respectively in the women's 50m rifle 3P individual final.The final medal count was impressive, but expectations around India's shooters were even higher.Badminton managed only one medal — a bronze in the men's team event.The result was underwhelming for a sport that has produced some of India's biggest Asian Games and Olympic stars.The campaign was also overshadowed by criticism of the Games' scheduling and organisation. H.S. Prannoy, who won the men's team bronze, described the experience as “sad” for athletes and criticised the accommodation and scheduling arrangements.Equestrian was another discipline that failed to make a mark for India at Aichi-Nagoya.Despite India's pedigree in the sport and its strong performances at previous Asian Games, the contingent returned without a medal.The result added to a list of disciplines where India was unable to convert participation and experience into podium finishes, making equestrian a relatively disappointing campaign.Several disciplines failed to make a significant impact for India at the Asian Games 2026. Esports was among the clearest disappointments, with India failing to win a medal across its events, while fencing and volleyball also ended without a podium finish despite sizeable contingents and expectations.Table tennis managed only one bronze, a modest return for a sport with India’s growing international stature, making it another underwhelming campaign.Rowing produced a solitary bronze, leaving the discipline with a relatively limited medal haul. Taken together, these results highlight the gaps India still needs to address beyond its stronger medal-producing sports.
Article Summary: India signed off from the Asian Games 2026 in fourth place with 85 medals — 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze. India won five gold medals, with the women's and men's compound teams, mixed compound team and Kumkum Mohod's individual recurve triumph providing the highlights. India's cricket teams delivered two more gold medals.

Article Title: As a manager, it’s important to use common sense: Diego Forlan
Article Text:

Kolkata:

TOI

Diego Forlan won’t have pleasant memories of his last visit to Kolkata. It was a decade ago, when as captain and marquee player of Mumbai City FC , the Uruguay star battled for a place in the Indian Super League (ISL) final against Atletico de Kolkata, only to petulantly pick up a red card.Atletico de Kolkata went on to clinch a five-goal thriller, and Forlan’s second-half sending off killed Mumbai’s chances.“I was disappointed because I think if I weren’t sent off in that game, we should have won,” Forlan tells, slightly sheepish. “We played them a couple of times and won quite well. We were the best team (at the end of the league stage).”Forlan returns to Kolkata on Tuesday for a friendly against India. This time he’s the Uruguay coach, tasked with improving the nation’s fortunes after a disastrous World Cup, where they were knocked out in the group stage after picking up two points from three games.“It’s a privilege to coach Uruguay, regardless of the circumstances. I don’t know if it’s the right time. I had the opportunity and I took it up. Uruguay is a great national team, with great players, and till I am the coach, I will try to enjoy every game.”Forlan has taken over the team’s charge from Marcelo Bielsa, possibly football’s most philosophical coach. Bielsa’s stint started with plenty of promise as Uruguay defeated Argentina and Brazil in away games. But the team later disintegrated, eventually ending in a “very painful” exit.By Bielsa’s own admission, nobody seemed interested in what he said.Forlan is unlikely to face such a mutiny. After all, he’s a Golden Ball winner at the FIFA World Cup 2010 and the country’s most decorated footballer.“Just because I won the Golden Ball, it does not mean that everything I say or do will be correct,” says Forlan. “I’m human and I know things are right and wrong. I try to use common sense (while coaching). I work with the players, try to have a good group, enjoy what they are doing.“Of course, as manager, I will have a way of playing, a way of trying to do things. As (a former) player, the advantage is of experience. You know how to use your experience because you understand the players better. You know everything. It’s important to use common sense.”Uruguay has a rich footballing history, deeply embedded in the national culture. A country of just three million people, there is a remarkable sense of close-knit community and underdog spirit that bonds its national team. Uruguay rarely gives an inch on the field, and, in the eyes of some, carries a ‘dirty’ image.Forlan sees it differently.“People talk about the way we play but I think sometimes it’s a little bit mistaken. It’s not that we are rough; it’s the way we play till the end of the game, doesn’t matter who we are up against. We know every game will be very difficult, but we will make it even more difficult for our opponents. That’s how we play. That’s the spirit we carry on the field.”Forlan’s appointment as interim coach ends next March. He does not have the luxury of counting upon the expertise of Uruguay’s most famous striking duo of Luis Suarez and Edinson Cavani, who between them have 280 international appearances. Playing alongside both, the coach has fond memories, but feels it’s time to move ahead“I enjoyed playing with them and as a Uruguayan fan, I enjoyed watching them with the national team, scoring many goals in different World Cups,” says Forlan. “Now, we don’t have to think how we can fill the gap (after their retirement). In life, nobody will stay forever. We need to adapt, see that life doesn’t stop with someone.”
Article Summary: Uruguay face India in a friendly in Kolkata on Tuesday. Diego Forlan is the interim coach of the national team. Forlan won the Golden Ball at the FIFA World Cup 2010. He says he will use 'common sense' while coaching Uruguay.

Article Title: From suspicion to devotion: Lionel Messi's long road from 'outsider' to Argentina’s undisputed leader
Article Text:
Lionel Messi

A love under construction

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

When Lionel Messi makes his final appearance for Argentina against Benin on Tuesday at Buenos Aires’ Monumental stadium, it will mark the end of an international career that has lasted more than two decades.It will also bring the curtain down on a relationship that took time to develop. Argentina’s football authorities once struggled even to identify the teenage Messi, who was developing his career far from home. Over the years, he went from being viewed with suspicion to becoming the leader of the national team and one of the most important figures in Argentine football."He went through so many moments that they're really very different eras. At first he suffered enormously with the national team. He truly endured it," Argentine journalist and author Sergio Levinsky, who wrote "Messi and Everything Else", told news agency Reuters.Messi moved to Barcelona as a teenager. While Spain tried to convince him to play for them, Argentina had limited knowledge of the youngster from Rosario.At the 2003 Under-17 World Cup in Finland, Spain beat Argentina 3-2 after extra time in the semi-finals.According to Levinsky, Cesc Fabregas, who scored twice in the match and was Messi’s teammate at Barcelona’s La Masia academy, told Argentine delegates after the game: "You lost to us because we've got your best player at Barcelona and he's a genius."Argentina youth coach Hugo Tocalli recalled a similar conversation. Speaking at the Ole Summit last month, he said Spain’s head chef told him Argentina needed "a kid who plays in Barcelona" to win the tournament.The Argentine Football Association (AFA) then had to find the teenager who was already making an impression in Spain.AFA employee Omar Souto tracked down the Messi family through a Rosario telephone directory, but when he made contact, he asked for "Leonardo"."His name isn't Leonardo, it's Lionel," Souto was told, according to the documentary "Messi: The Forgotten Tape".Even Messi’s name caused confusion in the paperwork. Levinsky said the AFA sent Barcelona a fax asking about a player called "Mecci", spelling the surname with a double "c" because officials believed he might be Italian.Messi eventually played two under-20 friendlies for Argentina in 2004, making his first appearances in the blue and white shirt. But doubts about him remained.At the 2005 Under-20 World Cup in the Netherlands, Messi started on the bench as Argentina lost their opening game."There was strong resistance to calling up a kid who didn't play in the country," Levinsky said, as quoted by Reuters. "He had to fight against those early suspicions, against being considered a foreigner because he lived in Spain."Messi was later criticised for not producing the same level of football for Argentina that he did for Barcelona. Some fans even labelled him "pecho frio", suggesting he lacked heart or fire.A World Cup qualifier against Colombia in 2011 became an important moment in changing that perception. Messi helped Argentina recover from a goal down in difficult conditions."He was exhausted, even vomiting, and he ended up winning," Levinsky said. "It was the first time fans saw him differently."The relationship grew stronger after Messi briefly retired from international football following Argentina’s penalty shootout defeat by Chile in the 2016 Copa America final. Instead of blaming him, Argentine fans publicly urged him to return."People realised he was not responsible for the defeats. He was the one getting them to finals," Levinsky added.Under Lionel Scaloni, Messi became the clear leader of a new generation of Argentine players. He guided the team to two Copa America titles and the 2022 FIFA World Cup.As Messi became a more vocal captain, comparisons with Diego Maradona became inevitable. But Levinsky believes the debate over who was Argentina’s greater player misses the bigger picture."It is Messi and Maradona," he added. "They were both geniuses in different eras.""Messi was like suddenly finding out you have an 18-year-old son," Levinsky said. "You have to start loving him without having known he existed. It was a love under construction."
Article Summary: Lionel Messi makes his final appearance for Argentina against Benin on Tuesday. Messi's international career has lasted more than two decades. Argentina’s football authorities once struggled even to identify the teenage Messi. He went from being viewed with suspicion to becoming the leader of the national team.

Hugo Porfírio once shared dressing rooms with some of Portugal's most recognisable footballers, played in the Premier League and La Liga, and appeared for his country at a major tournament. More than two decades after those playing days came to an end, his life looks very different, with the former Sporting and Benfica midfielder now finding himself behind the wheel of an Uber in Lisbon, where two passengers recently realised who had picked them up.Porfírio came through Sporting Lisbon's academy before making his senior debut during the 1992/93 season, when Bobby Robson gave him his first-team opportunity and he made two appearances.He played 13 matches and scored once during the following season before moving through loan spells at Tirsense and União de Leiria, experiences that eventually helped lead him towards a career outside Portugal.His next major move took him to West Ham, where he made 27 appearances, scored four goals and provided three assists while sharing the pitch with Portuguese great Paulo Futre.Porfírio later moved to Spain with Racing Santander, producing one of the more productive spells of his career with 23 appearances, two goals and three assists during the 1997/98 campaign.That form led to a move to Benfica in 1998/99, although his time at the Luz was interrupted by a loan spell at Nottingham Forest, where he played nine matches, scored once and contributed two assists.He returned to Benfica for the 1999/00 season and made six appearances, scoring once and providing two assists before moving to Marítimo on loan during the following campaign.At Marítimo, Porfírio featured 21 times, scored twice and supplied one assist before returning to Benfica for the 2001/02 season, when he made another six appearances.He subsequently played for Benfica B during the 2002/03 and 2003/04 seasons before moving to Oriental in 2006/07, eventually ending his playing career at Al-Nassr in 2007/08, the Saudi club where Cristiano Ronaldo and João Félix now also play.Porfírio's club career was accompanied by an international career that reached a level most professional footballers never experience.He represented Portugal three times at senior level, including an appearance at Euro 1996, while also making 10 appearances for the Portuguese under-21 side and scoring two goals.His senior international involvement placed him in the same dressing room as players including Rui Costa, Luís Figo and Vítor Baía, names who became central figures in one of the strongest generations of Portuguese football.Although Porfírio never accumulated the international appearances associated with those players, being part of that Portugal squad and appearing at a major European Championship remained one of the defining achievements of his playing career.Football did remain part of his life after retirement, although only briefly and in a very different capacity from his time as a player.He returned to Sporting during the 2011/12 and 2012/13 seasons, joining the coaching staff first under Ricardo Sá Pinto and later working with Oceano, including involvement with the club's B team.That period represented his final significant connection with professional football before his life moved in another direction.At 53, Porfírio is now working as an Uber driver, according to Portuguese media reports, a reality that came to wider attention after two passengers unexpectedly recognised him during a routine journey.According to, the former Portugal international was recognised at the wheel by influencer André Ramalho and a friend, who had turned to Uber after running late for what should have been a short walk between Olivais and Chelas.“We were walking because we were only going from Olivais to Chelas, which is a 10-minute walk, but we were a bit late, fell asleep, and had to call an Uber,” Ramalho said in a video.The passengers initially appeared to have expected an ordinary ride before realising that the driver had once played alongside some of Portugal's most famous footballers.“This guy is totally taking us for granted. What do you mean, nothing special? He played in Euro 1996, played with Rui Costa, Luís Figo, Vítor Baía. He's the coolest guy ever. Really cool. He drove well... I don't even know if football players are known for driving well,” Ramalho added.Porfírio maintains a private social media profile and has largely stayed away from public attention since leaving professional football, meaning the unexpected Uber encounter has offered one of the few glimpses into his life in recent years.The contrast with his playing career is striking, but the details of that career have not disappeared, with a Sporting academy education, spells at Benfica and West Ham, European football, a period in Saudi Arabia and three Portugal appearances forming the background to the man now taking passengers across Lisbon.For the two passengers who opened an Uber booking expecting a short ride across the city, however, the driver turned out to be someone whose football career belonged to a very different part of his life.
Article Summary: Hugo Porfírio played for Sporting Lisbon, Benfica and West Ham. The 53-year-old also played for Portugal at Euro 1996. He is now reportedly working as an Uber driver in Lisbon. Two passengers recognised him at the wheel during a routine journey.
